opus-5.5.text:
I think it becomes incontrovertible when it shows up in the work people actually do, and when we can measure that. For a long time the field has leaned on benchmarks that are a bit abstract, like multiple-choice exams, competition math, or puzzle-style tasks. Those were useful, but a lot of them are saturated now, and honestly, most people don't feel anything when a model scores 90 instead of 85 on some academic test. It doesn't map onto their lives.

So a lot of what I care about is building evaluations that look like real, economically valuable work. You take tasks from experienced professionals, like lawyers, nurses, engineers, financial analysts, people with years in their field. You have them create realistic deliverables, the kind of thing they'd actually hand to a client or a boss. Then you have other experts blindly compare the model's output against a human expert's output. When you see models starting to match or beat professionals on a meaningful share of those tasks, and doing it much faster and cheaper, that's a very different conversation. It's no longer "the model is good at trivia." It's "the model wrote a memo I would have accepted from a colleague."

I think the other part is personal experience. People become convinced when it solves their own problem. Someone uses it to understand a medical report, or debug something at work they were stuck on for days, or draft something that would have taken their whole afternoon. That moment is very persuasive, more than any chart we can publish.

So it's both of those together. You need rigorous, grounded measurement so the claims are credible and not hype, and you need people having those firsthand moments where it clearly helps. And I'd add that being honest about where models still fall short matters a lot too. If we're clear about the failure modes, people trust the claims about capability more.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s power will be evident in realistic work tasks and personal use, but it does not say people will recognize it by realizing how much of their work they use models for.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify anticipated scientific breakthroughs as a route to demonstrating AI models’ power.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it becomes incontrovertible when the models stop being something you evaluate and start being something you depend on. Right now a lot of people experience AI through a chat window, and the natural reaction is to poke at it, find the mistake, and say, "See, it's not that smart." That's fine, that's healthy skepticism. But the moment that shifts is when the model does a piece of work that actually matters to you, over a long horizon, and you realize you couldn't have done it yourself, or it would have taken you days.

A lot of my work is on evaluations, and one thing we've seen is that benchmarks saturate way faster than public perception updates. We'll build a hard eval, something that looks like real expert work, and within a year or two the models are at or past the human baseline. But for most people that's an abstract number on a chart. What makes it real is when it touches their own domain. A scientist sees a model propose an experiment they hadn't thought of. A software engineer hands off a multi-day refactor and it just comes back done. A doctor sees it catch something. Everyone has their own threshold, and it's usually "the thing I'm an expert in."

So I'd say it won't be one dramatic moment. It'll be a lot of individual, personal moments, where the model does something in your area of expertise and you can't dismiss it. And then economically, when you start seeing real tasks, real jobs, real scientific results that clearly came from these systems, the argument sort of ends on its own. The output speaks for itself.

r001.rationale: The response says people may depend on models for important work, but it does not clearly identify recognizing how much of their work they use models for as the route to recognizing their power.

r002.rationale: The response mentions scientists, experiments, and scientific results, but does not clearly predict scientific breakthroughs as a route to making the models’ power incontrovertible.

astra-6.text:
I think it becomes incontrovertible when it does something that matters to you personally—something you couldn’t do before, or that would have taken you weeks, and suddenly you can do it in an afternoon. You don’t need a benchmark to tell you that’s powerful. You’ve experienced it.

And that moment will look different for different people. For one person, it might be building a piece of software without knowing how to code. For someone else, it might be finally understanding a subject they’ve struggled with because they have something that can patiently explain it in a way that clicks.

I don’t think there’s necessarily one big moment where everyone becomes convinced. I think it’s a lot of those individual experiences, followed by being able to rely on that capability consistently. That’s when it stops being an impressive demo and starts changing what people believe they can do.

r001.rationale: The response says people will recognize AI’s power through personal experiences of doing something they could not do before or doing it much faster. It does not say they will realize how much of their work they use models for.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify anticipated scientific breakthroughs as a route to making AI’s power incontrovertible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it becomes incontrovertible when it does something that matters to you personally. You can see a benchmark or watch an impressive demo, but that’s different from bringing a problem you’ve been stuck on and having the model help you solve it.

And the threshold is different for everyone. For one person, it might be understanding a piece of code they couldn’t figure out. For someone else, it might be finally understanding a concept they’ve struggled with for years. I think those moments—where you can judge the result yourself, because you know the problem so well—are what make the capability feel real.

r001.rationale: The response says people will recognize AI’s power through personally meaningful problem-solving, but does not mention realizing how much of their work they use models for.
